title: Microprobe matrix: tail latency vs small-batch fairness study
body:
Purpose / motivation:
This doc captures a tightly scoped set of microprobes to understand how our continuous batching scheduler behaves when dominated by small-size requests (1–4 tokens) and medium-size requests (200–400 tokens). We care about tail latency (p99, p99.9) and fairness across request classes when we tune two knobs: max batch size and batching timeout. Previous runs showed good p50/p95 but p99.9 spikes under mixed traffic; this work tries to: (1) isolate scheduler-induced tail events, (2) validate fairness heuristics, (3) provide actionable tuning guidance for Dedicated pools.

Hypotheses:
- H1: Reducing max_batch_size for small-request lanes improves p99.9 for small requests but increases total GPU utilization and may harm medium request p95.
- H2: Increasing timeout (waiting longer to form batches) reduces wasted slots and improves throughput but increases p50 for small requests; there is a knee where p99/p99.9 degrades sharply.
- H3: Fairness by weighted dequeue (round-robin with weights) can reduce starvation of small requests without severe throughput loss if weights are tuned per-request-size histogram.

Test matrix (microprobes):
- Variables:
  - max_batch_size: [8, 16, 32, 64] (operating on the global pool plus per-lane override)
  - batching_timeout_ms: [2, 8, 20, 50]
  - fairness_mode: [none (FIFO), size-aware-weighted, deadline-aware]
  - traffic_mix: [all-small (90% 1-4 token), mixed (60% small, 40% medium), bursty-medium (30% small, 70% medium)]
  - KV-cache: [enabled, disabled]
- Hardware: single A100-40GB (dedicated test node) running runtime v0.22.3 with quantized llama-2-13b (8-bit q4) model variant.
- Traffic generator: local bench tool (bench/run-profile.sh) with request template set (prompt length distribution) and constant concurrency driver.

Probe plan (ordered):
1) Baseline: default scheduler (max_batch=64, timeout=8ms, FIFO) on mixed traffic, kv-cache enabled. Collect 30-minute run.
2) Max_batch sweep: run mixed traffic with timeout fixed at 8ms, fairness FIFO, max_batch ∈ {8,16,32,64}. Each run 15 minutes, back-to-back.
3) Timeout sweep: with max_batch fixed at the best-throughput value from sweep, vary timeout. 10–20 minute runs.
4) Fairness modes: for promising batch/time combos, benchmark size-aware-weighted and deadline-aware. Capture per-class percentiles and request reordering events.
5) Bursty patterns: rerun top 3 configs under bursty arrivals (500 qps windows) to surface preemption and queue-eviction events.
6) KV-cache toggles: run winners with cache disabled to see sensitivity (cache hits improve tail for medium requests by avoiding long decode).

Metrics to capture (must be in CSV/TSV per-run and also exported to metrics backend):
- p50, p90, p95, p99, p99.9, p99.99 per request class (small/medium)
- throughput (tokens/s, requests/s)
- GPU utilization (SM% / mem%), kernel stalls (if available from nvprof/perf)
- Batch occupancy distribution (histogram of actual batch sizes served)
- Queue length over time (per-lane)
- Number and duration of blocked requests (waiting time before batch starts)
- Fairness metric: ratio of median latency small/medium and K-S test on latency CDFs
- Packet of dropped/timeout requests (if any)
- Cost proxy: GPU-seconds per 1k requests

Profiling hooks and commands:
- bench runner flags: --prompts-file=profiles/mix_a.json --concurrency=120 --duration=900 --record-batches=true --emit-metrics=pushgateway
- runtime flags for experiments: --scheduler.max-batch-size=32 --scheduler.timeout-ms=8 --scheduler.fairness=size-weight --profiling=flamegraph,cpu,mempool
- collection: collect flamegraphs from `/var/tmp/runtime-profiles` and GPU traces from `nsys` for the 2 worst p99.9 windows.
- use eBPF probe (tracepoint: runtime/serve:batch_dispatch) to get timestamps for sample-to-dispatch latency.

Quick results summary (high-level findings from initial runs 2025-01-20 to 2025-01-28):
- Baseline (max_batch=64, timeout=8ms, FIFO): mixed traffic p99 small = 420ms, p99.9 small = 1.2s (sporadic), p95 medium = 550ms. GPU utilization ~72% average.
- Reducing max_batch to 16: small p99.9 dropped to 480ms (major improvement), p95 medium increased by ~12% (to ~620ms). Throughput (tokens/s) decreased 9%.
- Lowering timeout to 2ms with max_batch=16: small p50 improved (from 45ms to 30ms), but p99.9 regressed slightly in burst windows because batches didn't fill leading to dispatch jitter.
- Size-aware-weighted fairness (weight small=2, medium=1) produced the best compromise: small p99 dropped 25% vs FIFO; medium p95 increased 6% (acceptable).
- Discovered a pathological case: when medium requests have long decode tails (due to kv-cache misses), small requests are occasionally queued behind a partial batch waiting for medium requests; deadline-aware fairness with a short preemption window (10ms) prevented the worst tails.

Interesting traces and bottlenecks observed:
- Flamegraphs: scheduler loop shows spikes in lock contention on the batch-map when many tiny requests arrive simultaneously; lock hold time correlates with p99 spikes.
- GPU traces: long kernel queues form when many medium requests are dispatched in contiguous batches; this increases head-of-line blocking for subsequent small batches that arrive during kernel queue drain.
- Memory allocator churn: small-request-heavy runs show increased mempool allocation calls in runtime, which introduces small delays (~0.5–2ms) that compound at high concurrency.

Actionable tuning recommendations (first-pass):
- For Dedicated pools expected to serve majority small requests, set max_batch_small_lane=16, timeout_ms_small=5, enable size-aware-weighted fairness (small weight=2).
- Add a preemption path in scheduler: if a small request waits > threshold (30ms) and current forming batch contains medium requests, permit the small request to be promoted to next batch.
- Reduce central batch-map lock granularity: prototype per-lane maps to reduce contention (follow-up PR attached).
- Add a garbage-free allocation path for small request objects (object-pool) to remove mem alloc churn.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- What is the long-term cost tradeoff on Dedicated pricing with smaller batch sizes? Need to run 24h runs measuring GPU-seconds per 1k requests across real traffic traces.
- How sensitive are these recommendations to model size/quality (try 70B distilled vs 13B quantized)?
- Are there any interactions with the autoscaler (scale-up thresholds) when we prefer smaller batches? Does autoscaler misinterpret lower throughput as under-provisioning and scale unnecessarily?

Run artifacts and next steps:
- Artifacts (s3): s3://redwood-internal/serving-profiles/microprobe/microprobe-2025-01-20.tar.gz (includes raw bench logs, flamegraphs, nsys traces)
- Follow-up PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/748 (locks -> per-lane maps)
- TODOs:
  - [ ] Run full 24h cost-sensitivity test under mixed production trace (owner: Priya, due: 2025-02-12)
  - [ ] Prototype preemption window and test under bursty arrivals (owner: Samir, due: 2025-02-05)
  - [ ] Add bench mode to synthesize kv-cache-miss-heavy workloads (owner: Lina, due: 2025-02-01)

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally experimental with shorthand numbers. See linked confluence page for cleaned results and charts. If you reproduce, use bench/run-profile.sh with `--record-batches` and upload the `batches.csv` artifact for correlation.

Raw excerpt (example bench stdout snippet):
  [2025-01-22T14:02:11Z] bench: rps=420, concurrency=120, batch-mean=18.2, batch-p75=32, small-req-p99=0.482s, medium-req-p95=0.61s
  [2025-01-22T14:02:43Z] runtime: dispatch loop contended, lock-hold=2.7ms, queued-batches=3
  [2025-01-22T14:02:44Z] nsys: kernel-queue-depth spike -> 180 pending kernels, drain-latency 340ms

If you want to debug locally: quick repro commands (on the test node):
- git checkout microprobe-locks && ./deploy-dev.sh --image=canary && sleep 30 && bench/run-profile.sh --prompts-file=profiles/mix_a.json --duration=600 --concurrency=120 --emit-metrics=pushgateway
- collect profiles: sudo tar -czf /tmp/profiles.tgz /var/tmp/runtime-profiles && aws s3 cp /tmp/profiles.tgz s3://redwood-internal/serving-profiles/microprobe/

Acknowledgements: Priya for running the long sweeps, Lina for the bench harness fixes, Samir for the NVidia traces and lock-profiling.
